title: The world as a wall of sand
hookLine: saadho rachnaa raam banaaee: this creation the Lord made is passing like a dream (Gauri M9, ang 219)

cards: On a beach in summer, a child builds a castle. Towers, a moat, a shell on top for a flag. It takes all afternoon, and the child is completely serious about it.
Then the tide comes in. Some kids cry. Some shriek with delight and run to build again.
The adults watching smile, because they know what the child is only learning: the wall was never going to last.
Guru Tegh Bahadur reaches for a picture like this, a wall of sand, and asks a harder question: what are we building that's any different?

teach.h: RACHNAA: THE CREATION THE LORD MADE.
teach.b: His hymn in Raag Gauri opens saadho rachnaa raam banaaee. Holy ones, this creation the Lord has made.
Then, in paraphrase: one person perishes, and another thinks he will stay forever; it's a wonder that can't be described. Gripped by lust, anger and attachment, people forget the Lord.
They take the body to be permanent, when it's like a dream that comes in the night. Whatever is seen will pass, like the shadow of a cloud.
And the last line: Nanak has known the world as mithiaa, false, not lasting, and stays in the Lord's shelter. A dream feels completely real while you're in it.

teach.h: A CLOUD'S SHADOW ON A FIELD.
teach.b: A cloud's shadow crosses a field and is gone before you can walk to it.

The wall of sand, baaloo kee bheet, is the image he uses in a salok later in this block: carefully built, and not built to last. But the hymn isn't sneering at the world. It calls it the creation the Lord made.

Some readers hear mithiaa as false to lean on, because it won't last. The mistake the Guru points at is ours: treating the sandcastle as bedrock, then breaking our hearts when the tide comes. Think back to the Barah Maha.
Poh's warmth, Magh's bath, Phagun's bliss: none of those months stayed, and its closing said every one was blessed anyway.
Passing doesn't mean worthless. It means hold it like sand, gently, with open hands.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's Gauri shabad 'saadho rachnaa raam banaaee' in kirtan, and often hear his images of the dream, the cloud's shadow and the wall of sand as reminders to hold the world lightly.

o: a wall of sand built on the shore
the creation, what the Lord has made
a dream that comes in the night

games.q: the world as a wall of sand — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn calls the world worthless
it calls the world mithiaa, false, yet also the creation the Lord made; the mistake is treating it as permanent.
the hymn compares what we see to the shadow of a cloud
it crosses the field and is gone.
the hymn ends with Nanak staying in the Lord's shelter
knowing the world is passing, he rests in the shelter.

games.q: the tide is coming for the sandcastle you built all afternoon. what does the hymn say about the world we build?
o: build higher walls so it lasts.
it's passing like a dream; hold it lightly and take the Lord's shelter.
games.why: Nanak, the hymn says, has known the world to be passing, and stays in the Lord's shelter. passing doesn't mean worthless.

practice: Pour a little water slowly from one glass to another, or let sand or sugar run through your fingers; if you can't, picture a river or an hourglass.

Nothing in the stream stays still, and yet the stream is there, so breathe with it and let one thing you've been gripping too tightly loosen, just a little. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Rachnaa, the creation, what the Lord has made. In Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, it is passing, like a dream, a cloud's shadow, a wall of sand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rachnaa, creation, what is made. The hymn calls the world the rachnaa the Lord made.

carryVoice: Your line: passing, like a dream. When the tide takes something, there's still the next handful of sand. That's day five hundred eighty-one.
